HSTU (ICML 2024) already provides mechanisms for temporal preference modeling: pointwise SiLU attention, learned relative position/time biases, and multiplicative feature gating. Meta’s implementation adds learned bucketed time-gap bias to positional bias before the SiLU attention activation. These biases can learn temporal relevance without imposing universal recency decay; HSTU’s existing gate is not explicitly a short-/long-term intent selector. Sources: [original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152), [official implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/generative-recommenders/main/generative_recommenders/research/modeling/sequential/hstu.py).

Related work supports separating temporal signals from sequence order. GRUT (2025) models timestamps, intervals and item transitions, motivating sensitivity to preference shifts, though its text-generation architecture differs from HSTU. PerSRec (2026) compresses long histories into learnable tokens combined with recent interactions and explicitly describes applicability to HSTU. FuXi-β (2025) identifies relative temporal bias indexing as an efficiency bottleneck and proposes functional relative bias; its attention-free replacement would depart from the required HSTU backbone. Sources: [GRUT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13957), [PerSRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03479), [FuXi-β](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10615).

Experiment hypothesis: retain HSTU and jointly learn a gate between recent-history and broader-history representations, conditioned on observed time gaps and sequence features. Compare against relative temporal bias alone to establish whether the explicit gate helps. Use only timestamps available at prediction; do not assume the next interaction time is known. Persistent interest, transient intent and completed needs remain latent interpretations, not observed labels. This is a proposed single-network extension, not an established result for the four Amazon categories.
